extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants / principal investigators and research faculty (including early-stage investigators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points about NIH's NOT-OD-14-074 policy allowing previously unfunded A1 submissions to be entered as new A0s, and strategies/risks for applicants and reviewers under that policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: NOT-OD-14-074 policy — A1 → A0 allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective immediately, following an unsuccessful resubmission (A1) application, applicants may submit the same idea as a new (A0) application for the next appropriate due date. The NIH and AHRQ will not assess the similarity of the science in the new (A0) application to any previously reviewed submission when accepting an application for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core policy change enabling applicants to re-enter previously unfunded work as 'new' submissions; it removes NIH screening for similarity at acceptance. Applicants are encouraged to refine and strengthen submissions even though the application is treated as a new A0.

rubrics_metrics.name: New (A0) applications cannot include introductions or responses to prior reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a new (A0) application does not allow an introduction or responses to the previous reviews, the NIH and AHRQ encourage applicants to refine and strengthen all application submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot explicitly respond to past summary statements in an A0; any improvements must be incorporated without the formal 'Introduction' or point-by-point rebuttal that resubmissions allow. Plan revisions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers instructed to treat A0 as a new idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The resubmission of an idea as new means the application will be considered without an association to a previous submission; reviewers will be instructed to review it as a new idea even if they have seen it in prior cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH instruction to reviewers does not guarantee reviewer compliance — the post notes that the only practical way to make this happen reliably is to get a different study section and avoid overlapping ad hocs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section / ad hoc reassignment required to avoid carryover recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way this is remotely possible is to put it in a different study section and make sure there are no overlapping ad hocs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want your A0 truly judged as new, try to get a different study section fit and minimize reviewer overlap (e.g., different ad hoc reviewers). Otherwise reviewers who saw prior versions may recognize the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy monitoring is limited/impossible from acceptance records
rubrics_metrics.description: The way they did this, there is no way to assess the impact. They will never know how many supposed 'A0' apps are really A2, A4, A6, nor how many 'A1' apps are really A3, A5, A7…etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because NIH will not assess similarity at acceptance and applicants can't include an introduction, the agency cannot reliably monitor whether 'new' A0s are recycled resubmissions, so claimed impacts (e.g., helping early investigators) are hard to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endless queuing/resubmission possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: So, for all intents and purposes you can revise and resubmit your failed application endlessly. Maybe they will pick you up on the A6 or A7 attempt!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy effectively allows repeated attempts by alternating A0/A1 submissions. Expect more applications in the pipeline and potential lengthening of time-to-funding for some projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of disadvantaging genuine brand-new A0 applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: The real point here is that genuine brand new A0s will certainly be disadvantaged relative to A2-as-A0 apps. On average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications that have benefited from prior reviews (even if resubmitted as A0) may have an advantage over truly new ideas; plan strategy accordingly if you are an applicant with no prior review shaping your proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential negative impact on early-stage/new investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: We heard increasing concerns from the community about the impact of the policy on new investigators because finding new research directions can be quite difficult during this phase of their career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy could increase competition against inexperienced PIs who have fewer 'in the pipe' reworked proposals. The post suggests NIH could instead treat ESIs/NI as a pass-through category to avoid harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload and peer-review capacity concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The only thing I imagine they could monitor is the GINORMOUS spike in submissions they’re sure to get, and whether it creates an impossible workload for reviewers, and/or a disproportionate increase in triaging of ESI/NI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect increased submission numbers and strain on reviewers; this may lead to more triage, lower review quality, or increased variability. Applicants should anticipate longer queues and possibly noisier review outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triaging and fairness to ESI in triage decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Study sections are not supposed to let the burden of triage fall on ESI applications. So if about 40% of nonESI apps are discussed, then the same proportion of ESI apps are supposed to be discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor whether study sections are actually maintaining fair proportions for ESI discussion. If not, ESI applications could be disproportionately triaged despite policy intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion scores calibration (use of full range for discussed apps)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a criterion/impact score calibration issue... We have been instructed to recalibrate to use the entire scoring range just for the applications we discuss. This means that the worst of the discussed applications is going to get a seven or eight impact score, but the triage cutoff is usually around four impact score. ... So if you were triaged, the criterion scores are completely utterly meaningless concerning whether you should revise and resubmit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious interpreting criterion scores for triaged applications — they may not reflect absolute quality. The post suggests this practice undermines criterion scores' informative value and raises the idea of abolishing them or changing scoring practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring variance and reviewer/sample noise
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose the omnipotent 'objective' score for your proposal is X. We all know that in a sample of judgments about that score, there will be variance around X... So why do people assume the best score is the true one and the worse score must be sign of bad review? Maybe it is just that the distribution of scores for your idea is being expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize inherent randomness/variance in scores across review rounds. Use that perspective when deciding whether to resubmit rather than assuming a single score is definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of 'messing up' a revision
rubrics_metrics.description: The application itself may not have changed much and may even have improved on many other aspects. But the mind of the reviewer interacts with the fact that there was an opportunity to respond to a reasonable critique and this opportunity was bypassed. This can fundamentally shift the confidence factor that what is being presented is good data versus a convenient crock-of-shit story based on cherry picking preliminary data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When revising, explicitly address reasonable prior critiques (when allowed) and perform necessary controls; failing to do so can worsen reviewers' confidence and score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic choice: resubmit triaged A0 as A0 (new) versus A1
rubrics_metrics.description: If we change the approach, is it better to re-submit as an A0 (as a 'do-over'), or submit as an A1, under the shadow of a previously triaged grant application? The only advantage to the latter that I can think of is the extra month of time we would have to generate sufficient preliminary data using the alternate approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider trade-offs: A0 avoids a formal association to the prior review but can't include a response; A1 lets you formally respond but may carry the negative history. Time to generate new data and magnitude of changes should guide choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion: keep A1 cutoff for twice-triaged grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Maybe they could keep the A1 cutoff for twice triaged grants? Throw two gutterballs in a row and that proposal is toast, no do-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One proposed policy to reduce recycling of chronically noncompetitive grants is to forbid new-A0 conversion after two triages. This is a debated remedy rather than current NIH policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring relative vs absolute and percentile calculation issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentile is not just based on scored grants, it is based on all grants, right? ... It doesn’t make sense that the worst discussed grant is scored a 9. It is likely better than a bunch of non-discussed grants. There were a bunch of calibrations that shifted scoring of some grants down, but the scores were never meant to be relative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that scoring practices and recalibration across cycles affect percentiles and funding comparisons; relative scoring shifts can advantage or disadvantage grants depending on the cohort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal to change review mechanics: single-criterion reviewers / MMI-style
rubrics_metrics.description: I think the criterion scores should be scored separately, by more reviewers. And one reviewer only assessing one criterion. Like MMI (multiple-mini interview) admissions interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a suggested reform to reduce bias and increase precision (e.g., blind assessment of Approach). It's not policy — consider it as a proposed way to improve criterion scoring reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice to applicants: improve grantsmithing and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: When overworked and inattentive reviewers encounter an exciting well-written grant, they manage to overcome their fatigue and give the grant the attention that it deserves. When they encounter a boring and/or difficult-to-read grant, they just shut down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write grants to be reader-friendly and compelling; this mitigates effects of overworked reviewers. Also seek ad hoc reviewer experience to understand panel behavior and improve your submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer factual errors and applicant recourse
rubrics_metrics.description: I have not yet received a summary statement that lacked a blatant factual inaccuracy about the document that the reviewers were supposedly considering... The big shots say they are too busy to handle their responsibilities ... so get out of the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual errors occur and can materially affect outcomes. Applicants should talk to program officers if needed, and understand that occasional errors are part of the system — submit more proposals and work to write clearly to reduce misreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation that stronger grants get more reviewer effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Save your powder for the grants that are at least decent. I spend very little time on grants I consider to be in the bottom half. Our job is to provide as large a spread of scores as possible to the discussed grants and thereby convey our relative ranking of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your grant is poor or poorly written, reviewers may not invest time; prioritizing clarity and significance helps ensure reviewers engage with your proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queueing effect on time to funding
rubrics_metrics.description: We’ll be seeing more queuing of apps... You’ll go A0, A1, A0, A1. At least under the two-shots rule, you had reviewers who would overlook petty problems they found in the Approach of an A1, because they knew that was the last try. Now, such reviewers can be as petty as they like and just assume it will be back soon as an A0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect longer chronological queues and possible shifts in reviewer incentives; strategize submission timing and study section selection to manage queue risks.
